metric_rationale: This metric isolates the specific incongruent trials (Trials 1 and 2) where Tallying and WADD make opposing predictions. On these trials, one option wins on 3 weak features while the other wins on 2 strong features. Tallying ignores feature validities and strictly prefers the option with 3 winning features. WADD weighs features by their validity, thus favoring the option with the 2 stronger features. By calculating the proportion of choices that align with the Tallying prediction on these specific trials, we expect a high score for data simulated under Tallying and a low score for data simulated under WADD.

This metric isolates trials 1 and 2, where one option has the two most valid features ([1, 1, 0, 0, 0]) and the other has the three least valid features ([0, 0, 1, 1, 1]). Tallying simply counts the number of winning features, so it will strongly prefer the option with three features (leading to a choice rate of [1, 1, 0, 0, 0] near 0, plus lapse noise). In contrast, WADD weights features by validity; the combined validity of the top two features (0.95 + 0.90 = 1.85) outweighs the bottom three (0.60 + 0.55 + 0.50 = 1.65), meaning WADD will frequently choose the option with only two features. Measuring the selection rate of the [1, 1, 0, 0, 0] option on these specific trials provides a massive, stable dissociation between the two theories.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Take-The-Best (TTB) heuristic specifically on incongruent trials, where the choice predicted by the single most valid discriminating feature opposes the choice predicted by a compensatory weighted sum of all features (WADD). TTB simulated subjects will exhibit a high proportion of TTB-aligned choices, whereas WADD simulated subjects will exhibit a low proportion, providing a strong and direct dissociation.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Take-The-Best (TTB) heuristic's prediction. TTB decides based on the single most valid discriminating feature. The experimental design includes many incongruent trials where the single best cue points to one option, but the sum of all other cues points to the alternative. Consequently, data simulated under TTB will show a high consistency rate with this metric, whereas data simulated under the Weighted Additive (WADD) theory will show a significantly lower consistency rate, yielding a strong quantitative dissociation.

This metric computes the difference in the probability of choosing the Take-The-Best (TTB) winner between trials where Tallying strongly supports the TTB winner (TTB winner has 4 positive features) and trials where Tallying strongly opposes the TTB winner (TTB winner has only 1 positive feature). Under the pure TTB theory, the number of supporting features is irrelevant, so this difference should be zero (subject to noise). Under the Hybrid model, the Tallying process will pull choices away from the TTB winner when support is low, and push choices toward it when support is high, resulting in a significantly positive difference.

This metric calculates the drop in the probability of choosing the Take-The-Best (TTB) winner as the number of cues favoring the opposing option increases. Under the pure TTB theory, the choice depends exclusively on the single most valid cue, so the number of opposing cues should have zero effect (the metric should be near 0). Under the Hybrid theory, the compensatory Tallying process increasingly favors the TTB loser as it accumulates more winning features, pulling the mixed choice probability away from the TTB winner. Therefore, the Hybrid model predicts a strictly positive difference (p_few > p_many).
